hints: Focus on what the shape of a Boltzmann curve tells you about temperature, taller and narrower versus shorter and broader.
The taller, narrower curve with its peak shifted to the left is the lower temperature curve, because fewer molecules have high energy.
Remember the most probable energy is read on the energy (x) axis directly below the peak of that lower temperature curve.
walkthrough:
**Spot which curve is the lower temperature**

Think of heating as spreading molecules out to higher energies. So the lower temperature curve is taller, narrower, and closer to the y-axis. That is the left-hand curve with the high peak.

Lower T = taller peak, Higher T = shorter, broader peak

**Recall what most probable energy means**

The most probable energy is the energy value possessed by the largest number of molecules. On a Boltzmann distribution, that is always the x-value at the very top of the peak.

**Read the correct letter from the axes**

For the lower temperature (taller) curve, drop vertically down from its peak to the energy axis. That foot lands on letter C, while the y-value of that peak is A.

options.A: A is on the y-axis, so it is a number of molecules (proportion / probability), not an energy. It is the peak height of the lower temperature curve, not its most probable energy.
options.B: B is also on the y-axis, so it cannot be an energy. It is the peak height of the higher temperature (shorter, broader) curve.
options.C: C is on the x-axis (energy axis) directly below the peak of the taller, narrower curve. That curve is the lower temperature, and the x-value at the peak is defined as the most probable energy.
options.D: D is on the x-axis below the peak of the shorter, broader curve. That is the most probable energy for the higher temperature sample, not the lower temperature.
